item.title: The interplay between cortical tracking and functional connectivity in musicians and non-musicians listening to speech and music
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Musical expertise is associated with auditory processing advantages which can extend to the speech domain. However, the origins of such domain-general benefits remain unclear. Recent frameworks propose that better rhythm processing in musicians might be at the basis of the observed advantages in processing music and speech. Auditory cortical tracking and inter-regional interactions between auditory and motor areas have been proposed as key neural mechanisms. In this study, we asked whether expertise-related increase in cortical tracking would be elicited by naturalistic stimuli in clear listening conditions, and whether such effects would be related to audiomotor functional connectivity and individual rhythmic abilities. We compared MEG data from expert musicians and controls with no musical playing experience while they listened to two-minutes long stories and excerpts of piano music. We also collected behavioral data in a rhythmic task testing speech (syllable) production. We found that musicians showed enhanced tracking and enhanced functional connectivity in both speech and music conditions, as well as better rhythmic abilities relative to non-musicians. Alpha connectivity between the right auditory cortex and inferior frontal gyrus negatively predicted cortical tracking across all participants in the speech condition, while no relation was observed for music. We suggest that stronger cortical tracking in musicians is due to domain-general differences in auditory sensory processes and is not driven by motor influences in our experiment. Moreover, a trade-off between cortical tracking and inter-regional communication might be at the basis of optimal perception of speech in both musicians and non-musicians in clear listening conditions.

item.title: Naturalistic Movie Viewing Reveals a Distributed Network Supporting Audiovisual Speech Processing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Traditional paradigms in cognitive neuroscience often fail to capture the richness of real-world experiences. To bridge this gap, researchers increasingly use naturalistic stimuli such as movies, which provide complex, multisensory input. Speech perception is a prime example of such complexity: it is inherently multisensory, involving the integration of auditory cues, lip movements, and facial expressions. Prior studies suggest that the left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and superior temporal gyrus (STG) play a critical role in this integration. However, most studies of audiovisual speech have relied on simplified or artificial stimuli, limiting ecological validity. To address these gaps, we analyzed fMRI data from human participants watching two full-length films (500 Days of Summer, Citizenfour) to assess the consistency of multisensory speech processes across distinct genres and narratives. We manually annotated word onset times and modality (audiovisual vs. auditory-only). Across two movies and 38 participants we observed consistent speech-related activation in the pSTS and STG across speech types. Compared to auditory-only speech, audiovisual speech recruited a broad left-lateralized network including the angular gyrus, posterior temporal cortex, temporal pole, and inferior frontal gyrus, along with the right cerebellum. These findings were also consistently present in single-subject data. Importantly, most of the regions observed in our analyses have been implicated in multisensory function in the nonhuman primate literature despite receiving relatively little focus in human neuroimaging. Together our results demonstrate that speech processing during naturalistic viewing recruits a distributed network extending substantially beyond regions traditionally emphasized in audiovisual speech research.

item.title: Brain Dynamics of Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness at Rest Reveal Alterations in Multisensory and Motor Areas
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Persistent Postural-Perceptual Dizziness (PPPD) is a chronic functional disorder with unsteadiness and postural instability, attributed to altered multisensory integration and visual dependence. fMRI studies report altered connectivity in several regions, however, dynamic connectivity remains unexplored. Objectives We characterized resting-state brain dynamics in 17 patients with PPPD and 20 matched healthy controls (HC), and their relationship to clinical and postural measures. Methods Co-Activation Patterns (CAPs) were derived from resting-state fMRI scans for four seeds relevant to multisensory integration, motor output and vestibular processing - right temporo-parietal junction (rTPJ), caudate nucleus, hippocampus and operculo-parietal area 2 (OP2) - and their temporal metrics compared between groups. Partial Least Squares Correlation (PLSC) related CAPs to mood, vertigo, stress, and visual dependence for gait and postural control. Results Patients with PPPD showed altered dynamics seeded from rTPJ (decrease of a salience-coupled CAP, increased entries into a visual/dorsal-attention-coupled CAP), caudate nucleus (increased time in a default mode-coupled CAP, decrease of a salience/visual-coupled CAP) and hippocampus (increase of a default-mode-coupled CAP), but not OP2. PLSC yielded two significant latent components: the first linked rTPJ, OP2 and hippocampal CAPs sharing visual network co-deactivation to stress, mood, vertigo and visual dependence for gait; the second linked all caudate and two rTPJ CAPs to postural sway with eyes closed (visual dependence). Individual brain-behavior scores correlated in both groups. Conclusion Resting-state dynamics are altered in multisensory and motor regions in PPPD, but preserved in OP2, the core vestibular cortex. Brain-behavior organization appears shared across groups, with shifted dynamics in patients.

item.title: Impact of hearing loss on visual selective attention: Evidence from N2pc and resting-state networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Efficient visual attention is fundamental to environmental adaptation and social interaction. While previous studies have observed alterations in visual processing among deaf individuals, findings remain controversial regarding whether these changes stem from hearing loss (sensory compensation vs. cognitive deficit) or sign language experience. To address this issue, the present study provides task-related and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) evidence to disentangle the specific drivers of visual selective attention plasticity. A visual search task was used to examine selective attention in 95 participants (34 prelingual deaf, 27 hearing signers, and 34 hearing nonsigners). Compared to both hearing groups, deaf individuals exhibited significantly lower hit rates and diminished N2-posterior contralateral (N2pc) amplitudes. Hearing signers and nonsigners showed comparable behavioral performance, N2pc amplitudes, and resting-state network topology, whereas the deaf group was further characterized by a degraded resting-state alpha network topology, evidenced by reduced clustering coefficients, global efficiency, and weakened frontal-occipital connectivity. N2pc amplitude correlated significantly with resting-state network properties and behavioral accuracy. These results suggest that deaf individuals may suffer from an imbalance in the regulation of visual selective attention, most clearly indexed by the evoked N2pc and by intrinsic alpha-network organization, and likely linked to increased resource competition following the loss of auditory monitoring. Our findings provide neurophysiological evidence that these attentional deficits are associated with hearing loss rather than with sign-language experience, offering a new perspective for understanding the boundaries of cross-modal plasticity in the human brain.

item.title: Prefrontal Cortical Changes With Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement in Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
Despite decades of clinical implementation of medications for opioid use disorder (OUD), overdose mortality rates remain high, underscoring a critical need for interventions that target the brain mechanisms underlying addiction. To assess the neural mechanisms of Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) and their associations with clinical outcomes, including craving and abstinence duration. This randomized clinical trial was conducted from November 2020 to September 2024 among individuals with OUD recruited from an inpatient rehabilitation facility in New York and randomized to MORE or psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST). Data were analyzed from October 2024 to August 2026. Treatment with MORE (comprising training in mindfulness, drug cue reappraisal, and savoring positive experiences) or PST (active control condition) across 8 weekly 2-hour group sessions. Outcomes included treatment-related changes in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood oxygen level-dependent signal (primary), abstinence length (secondary), and cue-induced craving (secondary). Drug cue reactivity task analyses included 59 participants (MORE, n = 24; 5 women [20.8%]; mean [SD] age, 43.6 [11.3] years; PST, n = 35; 8 women [22.9%]; mean [SD] age, 42.8 [10.0] years). Movie-watching and follow-up analyses were conducted in subsets of 37 (MORE, n = 18; PST, n = 19) and 38 participants (MORE, n = 13; PST, n = 25), respectively. Compared with PST, MORE reduced drug-biased activity in the middle frontal gyrus and other brain areas, including the precuneus, during downregulation of responses to drug cues relative to upregulation of responses to natural reward cues (even when controlling for passive cue viewing; z > 3.1; P < .05). The shift from drug to natural reward responses in the lateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) was associated with lower cue-induced craving exclusively in the MORE group (z > 3.1; P < .05). Relative to PST, MORE also reduced medial PFC synchronization to naturalistic drug-related movie scenes (q = 0.019) and significantly extended abstinence duration at follow-up (approximately 4 months posttreatment; χ2 = 6.7; P = .04; Cohen w = 0.19). This neuroimaging randomized clinical trial demonstrates that MORE may restructure function in PFC nodes of the reward, salience, and control networks, positioning it as a biologically grounded adjunct to pharmacotherapy for OUD. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04112186.

item.title: Cerebello-basal ganglia networks and behavior across adulthood and aging
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The cerebellum contributes to aging, cognition, and reward related processing, but has been relatively understudied in these domains. The cerebello-basal ganglia (CB-BG) circuit may be key to better understanding how the brain ages. Prior work has implicated this circuit in aging in a small sample, though it is also of interest in age-related neurodegenerative disease, particularly Parkinson's Disease. Here, we investigated the CB-BG network, which has been implicated in modulation of cognitive, motor, and reward-related functions. In a sample of 138 participants between the ages of 35 and 86 we looked at network connectivity in cognitive and motor sub-circuits. Participants completed motor and cognitive testing batteries followed by 26 minutes of resting state functional connectivity magnetic resonance imaging (fcMRI). This data was analyzed using the CONN toolbox with an ROI-ROI approach targeting the CB-BG circuit. We replicated the previously mapped cognitive subcircuit and motor subcircuits. When examining connectivity by age group (early and late middle age and older adult hood), we found higher functional connectivity in early middle age compared to older adulthood, with no results related to late middle age. Analysis of connectivity as it relates to performance on the Stroop task showed higher connectivity-behavior associations in early middle-aged adults compared to older adults. We also explored sex differences and found higher functional connectivity in females compared to males. Analysis of steroid hormone levels revealed higher connectivity associated with progesterone in females relative to males. Together, we have replicated motor and cognitive CB-BG subcircuits and further demonstrated that this network has altered connectivity associated with age, sex, progesterone, and cognitive performance. This expanded investigation of CB-BG networks represents an essential new step in increasing our knowledge of age-related cognitive and motor declines and may be particularly relevant for consideration in Parkinson's Disease.

item.title: Insula functional connectivity development follows a canonical antero-posterior axis of organization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The insula is a heterogeneous region associated with a range of functional domains including sensory, cognitive, and emotional processing. Cytoarchitectural and functional studies have described an antero-posterior axis of insula organization. However, the insula's functional development remains sparsely described. We delineated the development of insula resting-state functional connectivity across 562 individuals (6-22 years) using generalized additive models and population value decomposition. We show insulo-cortical functional connectivity development differs across the insula: anterior subregions have predominantly decreasing connectivity across the age range examined, whereas posterior subregions have variable connectivity that aligns with the sensorimotor-association axis. Vertex-level analysis revealed that age-related trajectories followed an antero-posterior axis that aligned with estimates of insula microstructure. Our results emphasize that the development of insula connectivity is spatially heterogeneous and aligns with known cytoarchitecture. The normative insula development described here provides a foundation for investigating how emerging psychopathology may be linked to variation in insula development.

item.title: Familiarity synchronizes brain rhythms during natural viewing
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Our perception of the world is shaped not only by sensory information, but also by prior experience. However, how familiarity alters the coordination of neural representations across distributed brain networks remains unclear. Rhythmic neural activity provides a potential mechanism for coordinating information across sensory and higher-order brain regions in the light of previous experience. Here, we thus investigated whether familiarity alters the coordination of brain rhythms during naturalistic viewing. Participants who were either familiar or unfamiliar with the television series Game of Thrones viewed clips from the series while EEG or fMRI was recorded. We calculated the intersubject correlations of neural activity across EEG frequency bands and related this rhythmic activity to fMRI BOLD responses. Across participants, all brain rhythms showed reliable intersubject synchrony and related to activity across large-scale brain networks. Familiarity selectively enhanced intersubject synchronisation in beta and gamma rhythms, with these effects reflected in visual and default mode brain regions. Moreover, beta and gamma band activity were modulated by similar aspects of the movie, suggesting coordinated familiarity-related processing. These findings show that familiarity selectively shapes rhythmic neural dynamics across the cortex, providing a mechanism through which prior experience alters the coordination of neural representations during naturalistic perception.

item.title: Evaluating the mobile MUSE EEG headband for studying resting state EEG and event-related potentials
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
We examined whether and how tactile EEG experiments could be done through self-assessments by participants at home or through online experiments with consumer-grade mobile EEG devices. As a first step towards this aim, we performed a Flanker task in an online scenario with a MUSE headband and similarly a conventional lab experiment with a standard EEG device.Five undergraduate students participated in a visual flanker experiment and associated ERP components were recorded with either a standard 32-channel EEG System or a 4-channel MUSE EEG headband. In addition, we performed a 2-minutes resting state recording.Resting state brain oscillations measured with the Muse device revealed a similar pattern as with a standard EEG machine, however, strength of alpha oscillations was significantly reduced. For the Flanker task, in the Muse data, the stimulus-locked ERP components were less visible as compared to standard EEG, still the N200 was clearly expressed for the correct trials. Interestingly, in the incorrect trials, time-locked to the response there was the same negative Ne component visible as for the standard experiment. Our results reveal that the Muse device is suitable to obtain event-related potentials – even from interpolated electrode channels. Advanced preprocessing and artifact removal algorithms specifically targeting such devices with only a few and peripheral channels might help to better isolate ERP components of interest. It remains the challenge to develop devices and procedures for online tactile testing.

item.title: Neuroimaging Correlates of Adolescent Substance Use: A Systematic Review of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background: Neuroimaging may help characterize brain and contextual factors associated with substance use during development. The ABCD study supports investigation of developmental pathways relevant to substance use [1]. Objective: To synthesize original ABCD publications examining MRI measures in relation to substance use and substance-related exposures. Methods: The authors screened all 2,700 publications in the ABCD corpus. Original empirical articles reporting an MRI measure of any modality and a substance use variable were eligible; methodological, conceptual, review, and commentary articles were excluded. Imaging modality, brain measures, substances, design, and association direction were extracted for descriptive synthesis. Results: The evidence considered spans morphology, white matter microstructure, resting-state connectivity, and task activation. Findings concerning youth initiation, prenatal exposure, and familial liability address distinct developmental questions. Family history and stressful life events feature in the white matter literature [2]. Findings vary by modality, exposure definition, and temporal direction, and include null associations. Conclusions: The literature suggests distributed and context-dependent neuroimaging associations. Observational designs, overlapping participants, confounding, and analytic heterogeneity limit causal interpretation and assessment of independent replication. The findings support further longitudinal investigation but do not establish a validated MRI screening tool.

item.title: Impairment of mental time travel in patients with depressive disorders: Neural mechanisms and individual-level identification based on default mode network connectivity
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Mental time travel (MTT) enables re-experiencing past and pre-experiencing future events. Impairment in MTT is a core cognitive feature of major depressive disorder (MDD), but its neural mechanisms involving default mode network (DMN) functional connectivity remain unclear. Methods Thirty-six MDD patients and 36 healthy controls (HC) completed an adapted Autobiographical Memory Test to assess MTT. Resting-state fMRI examined DMN functional connectivity. Brain–behavior correlations used Spearman rank with Holm–Bonferroni correction. A support vector machine (SVM) classifier and support vector regression (SVR) evaluated individual discriminative and predictive values of identified connectivity features. Results Patients showed significantly reduced specificity in past recall and future imagination, with lower emotional valence, field perspective, and intensity. Resting-state connectivity revealed dissociated DMN patterns: weakened right anterior supramarginal gyrus–frontal pole, left frontal pole–posterior parietal, and hippocampus–lingual/cerebellar connections; enhanced left medial prefrontal–occipital and dorsal medial prefrontal–frontal pole connections. In HC, frontoparietal connectivity correlated with visual perspective; in patients, enhanced prefrontal connectivity negatively correlated with negative valence. Machine learning achieved 94.4% accuracy (AUC = 0.971) in classifying MDD vs HC, with frontal pole connections most discriminative. DMN connectivity significantly predicted individual specificity and neutral valence. Conclusions MTT impairment in MDD reflects system-level DMN imbalance and functional reorganization, providing neural targets for interventions. High individual classification accuracy supports DMN connectivity as a potential biomarker.

item.title: The path from brain to words is rerouted in opioid addiction
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Whether spontaneous speech preserves how the brain encoded an experience is unknown. We tested this question in opioid use disorder (OUD), in which drug cues outweigh other rewards. Eighty-two people with OUD and 34 controls watched the opening of the film Trainspotting during functional magnetic resonance imaging, then retold it in their own words. Language-model analyses showed that people with OUD dwelt on craving, personal identification and recovery, devoting more of their retelling to drug scenes. In 65 participants with imaging, this speech bias tracked how strongly the brain had distinguished drug from non-drug scenes during viewing, in left frontoparietal cortex in controls but left temporal cortex in OUD. Direct comparison showed left accumbens coupling positive in OUD and negative in controls, and left superior frontal coupling weaker in OUD. Spontaneous speech thus carries a trace of neural encoding whose route depends on what the experience meant to the speaker.

item.title: Beyond reduced alpha power: a weaker temporal link between alpha and other brain rhythms in Alzheimer's disease
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Reduced alpha power is among the most consistently reported resting electroencephalography (EEG) features of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, alpha activity also interacts with other rhythms over time, a dynamic aspect that power measures do not capture. Whether AD weakens this temporal interaction, and whether such a change carries information beyond reduced alpha power, remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed public eyes-closed resting EEG from 29 healthy controls (HC), 36 patients with AD and 23 with frontotemporal dementia (FTD). After separating periodic from aperiodic activity, we tracked the aperiodic exponent and periodic theta, alpha, beta and gamma activity in consecutive 1-s windows. A vector autoregressive model predicted these five measures from the preceding window. Alpha's predictive contribution (Gα) was the increase in prediction error for theta, beta and gamma when the model was refitted without alpha as a predictor, with training and testing on separate time blocks of each recording. AD-HC differences were adjusted for age and sex, then for alpha expression (periodic alpha power) and signal quality (dynamic range and spatial reliability), with alpha self-persistence (alpha's carry-over between windows) as a benchmark. We also tested whether expression and Gα each added information about AD beyond the other. An exploratory Jansen-Rit-family circuit model examined whether expression and Gα can change partly independently. Results: Gα was lower in AD than in HC (adjusted difference in 10^3Gα, -3.19; 95% confidence interval -5.25 to -1.13; p = 0.0035), with a consistent direction across sensitivity analyses. Adjustment for alpha expression and signal quality retained 75.8% of this difference but only 4.4% of the self-persistence difference. Expression and Gα each added information beyond the other (Holm-adjusted p = 0.012 for both). FTD contrasts were inconclusive. In the circuit model, reducing local recurrent excitation lowered alpha expression without an estimated decrease in Gα, whereas reducing downstream input lowered Gα with a smaller change in expression. Conclusions: At the group level, the resting alpha abnormality in AD comprises two partly nonredundant dimensions: reduced expression and a weaker temporal link between alpha and subsequent multi-rhythm activity. Quantifying this temporal link may complement conventional spectral markers of AD.

item.title: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6-80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

item.title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

item.title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

item.title: Resting-state alpha scale-free dynamics predict individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values during free choice
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Values learned through reward can continue to influence choices guided by one's own preferences, such as which painting to hang, to an extent that varies across individuals. Because such preferences build up gradually across choices, their expression may depend on how well internally generated states are sustained over time, a property indexed by long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) in intrinsic brain activity. We tested whether resting-state alpha-band LRTC predicts individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values. Eighty-one participants learned through probabilistic feedback which of four abstract shapes tended to be rewarded, and then judged their preferences among these shapes and 11 new shapes without feedback. Alpha LRTC was estimated by detrended fluctuation analysis of resting-state electroencephalography recorded before, between, and after the tasks. A trial-level mixed-effects model showed that reward history influenced preference judgments and that this influence decreased with resting-state alpha LRTC: participants with weak LRTC chose high-reward shapes over new shapes on 75% of trials, whereas those with strong LRTC were close to indifference (54%). The relationship was distributed across the scalp, stable across recordings, and not explained by spectral power or learning performance. Resting-state alpha LRTC is thus related to how strongly reward-learned values are carried into preference-based choice. Given the view that stronger LRTC reflects a longer window over which internally generated states are integrated, the observed relationship could arise because the window is biased toward values built up through one's own choices, or because it attenuates values learned under a criterion that no longer applies; which account holds remains to be determined.

item.title: Somatotopic functional connectivity gradients in the monkey and human striatum.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Understanding the topographic and functional organization of the striatum-a key brain structure involved in motor control, learning, and cognition-is crucial for elucidating the pathophysiology of the neurological and psychiatric disorders associated to it, and for developing targeted therapies. While recent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies in humans and non-human primates have noninvasively characterized the brain-wide connectivity patterns of the striatum, its detailed somatotopic organization and the homology across species remains to be fully elucidated. We aimed to comprehensively characterize the somatotopic organization of the striatum in macaque monkeys based on functional connectivity patterns, and to assess the extent of homology or divergence of this organization between macaque monkeys and humans. Resting-state functional connectivity data were obtained from 11 anesthetized macaques using an ultra-high-field 7-tesla MRI scanner. Using two complementary approaches-seed-based analysis and connectopic mapping-we successfully delineated a distinct, regular volumetric somatotopic map within the macaque posterior putamen, a motor-related subregion of the striatum. This map exhibited a gradient encompassing the lower limb, trunk, upper limb, and face representations, predominantly oriented along the dorsal-ventral axis. The somatotopic gradient identified in macaques demonstrated a remarkable similarity with the corresponding gradient in the human posterior putamen, characterized using a publicly available resting-state functional MRI dataset. Furthermore, cross-species decoding analysis revealed that the somatotopy of the human posterior putamen could be accurately predicted using the anatomically aligned macaque somatotopic map obtained in this study as reference. In addition to this shared gradient organization, our seed-based analyses suggested non-gradient-like features in the human posterior putamen. These findings offer compelling evidence for the high evolutionary conservation of the major topographic organization in the primate posterior putamen, while pointing to species-specific divergence.

item.title: Disrupted brain network topology and structure-function coupling in non-specific low back pain.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Central nervous system mechanisms contribute to non-specific low back pain (LBP), with widespread alterations in brain function and structure reported. It remains unclear how these alterations propagate to brain network topology and structure-function coupling. In this cross-sectional study, 282 participants with non-specific LBP (mean ± standard deviation, pain intensity 4.3 ± 1.7 [0-10 numerical rating scale]; current pain duration 54 ± 105 weeks) and 71 pain-free controls underwent resting-state functional and diffusion-weighted MRI to derive functional and structural connectomes. Subgroups were analyzed by pain status during scanning and pain duration. The main graph-theory analysis revealed that participants with non-specific LBP had lower segregation (d = 0.39-0.45, P = 0.009-0.019) in the whole-brain functional network and higher integration (d = 0.30-0.38, P = 0.005-0.027) in the functional ventral attention network. Subgroup analysis showed that participants with chronic non-specific LBP had lower segregation (d = 0.48, P = 0.002) and higher integration (d = 0.45, P = 0.004) within the structural default mode network. By modeling functional connectivity using structural communication predictors in a multivariable linear regression, we identified structure-function decoupling in participants with non-specific LBP across the whole-brain (d = 0.25-0.28, P = 0.026-0.041), ventral attention (d = 0.28-0.32, P = 0.005-0.048), and default mode network (d = 0.22-0.24, P = 0.031-0.046), alongside complex regional patterns of both decoupling and hypercoupling. Explorative partial correlation analyses associated disability, rather than pain intensity, with differences in brain network topology and structure-function decoupling. These findings advance the mechanistic understanding of the severity and persistence of non-specific LBP, showing disrupted bottom-up attentional processing and self-referential circuitry, resulting in large-scale structure-function decoupling.

item.title: Low-dose ketamine modulates brain entropy in treatment-resistant depression: Results from two neuroimaging clinical trials.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background Several studies have reported entropy reductions in regions of the brain associated with affective-regulatory and reward- and motivation-related processes in patients with major depressive disorder. However, whether low-dose ketamine modulates this reduction remains unclear. Methods We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from two single-infusion low-dose ketamine trials. Data at baseline and 3 days after infusion were analyzed. In Trial 1, patients with treatment-resistant depression were randomized to receive 0.2 or 0.5 mg/kg ketamine or normal saline. In Trial 2, patients with treatment-resistant depression and suicidal ideation were randomized to receive either 0.5 mg/kg ketamine or 0.045 mg/kg midazolam. Sample entropy was calculated from the spontaneous blood oxygenation level-dependent time series of 166 regions of interest defined by the automated anatomical labeling atlas 3. Results In Trial 1, increased brain entropy was observed in the gyrus rectus, cerebellar vermis I/II, substantia nigra, red nucleus, and bilateral locus coeruleus after low-dose ketamine infusion. In Trial 2, the ketamine group exhibited higher brain entropy in the left amygdala compared with the midazolam group. Discussion Low-dose ketamine rapidly increases brain entropy (from baseline to day 3) in frontolimbic, cerebellar, and ascending neuromodulatory regions, including the gyrus rectus, cerebellar vermis I/II, substantia nigra, red nucleus, bilateral locus coeruleus, and left amygdala. Changes in brain entropy after low-dose ketamine infusion may be associated with its rapid antidepressant and antianhedonic effects, although this relationship requires further investigation.

item.title: Cellular and mitochondrial correlates of regional glucose metabolism in the human cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Regional differences in human brain glucose metabolism reflect local energy demands, but their cellular and mitochondrial determinants remain unclear. We combined [18F]FDG positron emission tomography in healthy human participants with estimates of cellular composition and mitochondrial density to unravel (sub)cellular correlates of heterogeneity in brain glucose metabolism. By correcting for RNA content and differential gene expression due to postmortem sampling, we addressed methodological shortcomings in multimodal neuroimaging integration. We introduce transcriptionally derived cytoarchitectonic maps of the human cortex that are consistent with histological findings, providing a biologically grounded framework for relating in vivo neuroimaging signals. Accordingly, mitochondrial distribution showed strong association with the intrinsic energy requirements at resting state. In contrast, relations between metabolism and neuronal composition were driven by sensory input and mitochondria-sparse thin-axon neurons, suggesting that stimulation-induced energy demand is met rather by neuronal processes that are independent of mitochondrial abundance to maintain efficient information processing.

item.title: Brain synchrony between interacting sibling pairs during real-time cooperation: an fMRI hyperscanning study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Siblings typically represent the longest-lasting social relationships. Second-person neuroscience provides a framework for studying the neural mechanisms of real-time, reciprocal social interactions. Yet, most studies have focused on simplified coordination tasks, limited brain regions, and did not investigate neural dynamics between siblings. In the first study investigating brain synchrony between siblings to date, we used fMRI hyperscanning to simultaneously record brain activity in 50 same-sex healthy young adult sibling pairs while they played a complex collaborative problem-solving Tetris game requiring continuous non-verbal complementary coordination. Brain synchrony was quantified using inter-subject correlation across 36 regions of interest (ROIs) of the social brain atlas. The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05). These regions were primarily located within the higher-level theory of mind subnetwork (including bilateral temporo-parietal junction, precuneus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex), and intermediate-level subnetwork (including anterior insula, inferior frontal gyrus). Greater synchrony in the left temporo-parietal junction significantly predicted better cooperative performance, suggesting that shared neural modelling of a partner's intentions supports effective collaboration. Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05). This study provides first evidence that real-time cooperation between siblings is supported by inter-brain synchrony in core social brain networks. We highlight the value of ecologically valid hyperscanning approaches for investigating neural mechanisms of cooperation in long-term relationships, advancing the field of relational neuroscience.

item.title: Resting-state functional brain changes in temporal lobe epilepsy with comorbid depression: A meta-analysis.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Objective To compare the differences in functional brain activity between patients with temporal lobe epilepsy comorbid with depressive disorder (TLE-D) and those with temporal lobe epilepsy without depressive disorder (TLE-ND) via a meta‑analysis of resting‑state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) studies, and to explore the functional brain activity features associated with depressive symptoms. Methods Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Wanfang Data from database inception to September 2026 to identify cross-sectional studies comparing rs-fMRI-derived differences in functional brain activity between patients with temporal lobe epilepsy comorbid with depressive disorder (TLE-D) and those without depressive disorder (TLE-ND). Eligible rs-fMRI metrics included regional brain activity indices and functional connectivity indices. A meta-analysis of studies reporting regional brain activity indices was performed using anisotropic effect-size signed differential mapping (AES-SDM). Due to their limited number, studies reporting functional connectivity indices were only described narratively. Study selection and data extraction were then completed, and a voxel-based meta-analysis of the included studies was performed with AES-SDM. Results A total of six studies yielding nine datasets met the inclusion criteria, involving 100 patients with TLE-D and 108 patients with TLE-ND. Meta-analysis showed that, compared with the TLE-ND group, the TLE-D group had significantly increased spontaneous brain activity in the right precuneus, right angular gyrus, right superior frontal gyrus, left middle frontal gyrus, and left cerebellum (analyzed via AES-SDM with an initial exploratory threshold of uncorrected voxel-level P < 0.005 and cluster size ≥10 voxels, and validated by leave-one-out sensitivity analysis). No brain regions with significantly decreased spontaneous brain activity were detected. Conclusion These exploratory findings suggest that, compared with patients with TLE-ND, patients with TLE-D show distinct patterns of functional brain activity in multiple key nodes of the default mode network, including the precuneus and angular gyrus, as well as in prefrontal-related regions. These differences may provide preliminary neuroimaging evidence for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying depressive symptoms associated with temporal lobe epilepsy.

item.title: Global synchrony moderates sad mood and is associated with emotional Stroop interference and somatic symptoms.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Mood-congruent attention in depression has been studied via emotional interference tasks, including tasks comparing responses to sad and happy stimuli. Mood induction offers a way to experimentally induce sad mood in non-clinical samples and examine its association with subsequent emotional interference, including Sad-Happy interference. Previous studies have separately linked resting-state global neural dynamics (synchrony, metastability) to depressive symptoms and attentional processing. However, whether individual differences in baseline global synchrony and metastability relate to how individuals respond to sad mood remains largely unclear. This study therefore examined the relationship between neural dynamics, sadder mood after induction, and Sad-Happy interference. Depressive symptoms also encompass somatic domains alongside cognitive-affective domains, though these are rarely distinguished in neuroimaging studies. We further examined whether baseline neural dynamics and their association with sadder mood and Sad-Happy interference were related to depressive symptoms (total, cognitive-affective, and somatic). Forty-eight non-clinical individuals completed resting-state neuroimaging, mood induction (sad or non-sad), and an emotional Stroop task. We found in a cross-sectional moderated mediation model that sadder mood after induction was associated with greater interference from sad compared to happy stimuli at medium and high levels of global synchrony, particularly in exploratory path models that included somatic symptoms. Findings suggest that individual differences in resting-state global synchrony may be a neural correlate of sadder mood after induction and Sad-Happy interference in non-clinical individuals. This study offers preliminary associations linking neural dynamics, sad mood, emotional interference, and somatic symptoms, providing insights into the role of neural dynamics in emotional and attentional processing.

item.title: Age and sex impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity beyond symptom associations in persistent post-concussive symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
1. Objective to investigate whether resting-state EEG aperiodic parameters (i.e., offset and exponent) are associated with symptom burden and demographic factors in patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS) and differ from healthy controls. Methods In this cross-sectional observational study, resting-state eye-closed high-density EEG was recorded in patients with PPCS and in age-matched healthy controls. Aperiodic parameters were extracted from EEG power spectra. In patients, hierarchical multiple linear regression models included age and sex as a base model, with additional demographic and clinical symptoms entered separately. Patient-control differences were assessed using multiple linear regression adjusted for age and sex. Results Seventy patients with PPCS (54 female; 39.57±12.21 y.; 109.5 [76.5; 196] days post-concussion) recruited from a concussion care pathway and 38 healthy controls (17 female; 39.61±13.57 y.) were included. In patients, younger age and male sex were associated with higher offset and exponent values (all p ≤.014). None of the additional demographic and clinical variables improved model fit beyond age and sex (all p ≥.143). After adjustment for age and sex, neither offset ( p =.898) nor exponent ( p =.100) differed between patients and controls. Conclusion Resting-state aperiodic EEG parameters were consistently associated with age and sex, but not with self-reported symptom burden or clinical characteristics in patients with PPCS. Not accounting for these factors may generate apparent group differences attributable, at least in part, to demographic variability. Significance Age and sex are important sources of inter-individual variability in resting-state aperiodic EEG activity and should be systematically considered when investigating such features. Highlights Age and sex significantly impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity. Aperiodic EEG parameters were not associated with symptom burden in persistent post-concussive symptoms. Aperiodic offset and exponent did not differ between patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms and healthy controls after adjustment for age and sex.

item.title: Post-Learning Reactivation of Memories for Naturalistic Continuous Experiences
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Memories are not static records of the past; rather, the act of remembering can change how an event is recalled. Intriguingly, several studies also suggest that memories may be reactivated during rest. However, reactivation has largely been studied for spatial tasks and discrete stimuli, and we know little about whether spontaneous reactivation occurs for long timescale naturalistic events and how reactivation affects retention. Using fMRI, we show that neural activity patterns in the hippocampus and the Default Mode Network during encoding of narrative events were spontaneously reactivated during rest. Contrary to predictions, reactivation did not strengthen recall of movie details, and instead exploratory analyses suggested that reactivation in the hippocampus was associated with more gist-like recall one week later. These findings support the idea that memories for complex events may be spontaneously reactivated, but they suggest that rather than simply strengthening episodic memories, reactivation might help transform them. Significance statement We tend to think of memory as a process of recording and later playing back those experiences during retrieval, but some prior evidence suggests the brain may use downtime to process memories to help consolidate them. This paper uses functional MRI to show that the brain activation patterns present while people view films are spontaneously reactivated afterwards during rest. While there was no evidence to suggest that this reactivation strengthened memories, reactivation may be associated with more gist-like memory one week later. These findings suggest that the resting brain processes memories for complex events, but the results call for theories that account for transformations of memories beyond strengthening.

item.title: Longitudinal fMRI reveals altered developmental trajectories of functional network organisation associated with adolescent cannabis use
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescence is a critical period of brain development during which the endocannabinoid system continues to mature. These developmental changes may contribute to age-related differences in the association between cannabis use and large-scale functional network organisation, yet this association remains incompletely characterised. We hypothesised that regular cannabis use would be associated with differential one-year changes in resting-state functional connectivity between adolescents and adults. Resting-state fMRI data at two time points, one year apart, were analysed from 66 participants (31 aged 16-17 years; 35 aged 26-29 years) including 29 with regular cannabis use and 37 age-matched cannabis-naïve controls. Seed-to-voxel analyses examined longitudinal changes in functional connectivity across age and cannabis-use groups. Year change, age × user-group interactions were identified in salience and default mode network connectivity, including divergent changes in anticorrelations with medial prefrontal, thalamic, cerebellar and juxtapositional regions. Directionality of effects differed by network and region. Additional main effects of user group were observed for executive control and associative striatal connectivity, with the cannabis-use group showing decreased positive connectivity and reduced anticorrelation, respectively. Changes in functional connectivity were developmentally dissociable and predominantly observed in regions contributing to attentional and transmodal processing. These findings suggest that cannabis may be associated with alterations in the maturational refinement of higher-order neural systems, potentially reflecting age-related differences in neurobiological sensitivity to cannabis exposure. Considering developmental stage may therefore be important for characterising cannabis-related neurobiological differences and may have implications for understanding age-dependent vulnerability to cannabis-related psychiatric outcomes.

item.title: Mapping Lifespan Functional Connectivity with Vision Transformer and Attention-Guided Trajectory Analysis.
item.description:
International journal of neural systems
Brain aging involves widespread reorganization of functional networks, yet characterizing these changes across the lifespan remains challenging. This study presents an innovative application of a Vision Transformer (ViT) to resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) functional connectivity for age group classification using the Human Connectome Project (HCP) Lifespan datasets. A ViT model was fine-tuned on [Formula: see text] ROI-to-ROI connectivity matrices to perform three binary age group classifications (Young versus Old, Adult versus Aging, Young versus Aging). The model achieved accuracies of 91%, 71%, and 93%, respectively, under five-fold cross-validation. To interpret model decisions, attention weight maps from the final transformer encoder layer were extracted using attention rollout and thresholded with a scree plot analysis, identifying 48 high-salience connections across 28 brain regions. These features were analyzed across the lifespan using generalized additive models (GAM), and k-means clustering of the trajectories revealed three dominant lifespan connectivity patterns: Age-Declining, Mid-Life Peaking, and Age-Increasing. This study demonstrates the viability of the ViT for functional connectome analysis and shows that attention-based interpretability combined with GAM trajectory analysis can enrich insights into age-related changes in brain network connectivity, offering a framework for interpretable brain-age modeling.

item.title: Adapted physical activity enhances cortical surface area and modulates functional connectivity of default-mode and frontoparietal networks in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Psychiatry research
Adapted physical activity (APA) may benefit patients with schizophrenia (SZPs), but neurobiological effects remain underexplored. We investigated whether a 16-week web-based APA program (e-APA) induces brain plasticity in SZPs and whether brain changes relate to cardiorespiratory fitness and clinical symptoms. In secondary analyses of a randomized controlled trial, 31 SZPs were assigned to e-APA (n = 16) or e-health education (e-HE, n = 15), matched to 23 healthy controls (HCs). Structural and resting-state functional MRI were acquired pre- and post-intervention to assess cortical surface area, thickness, and functional connectivity (FC). Relationships with VO2max and symptom changes were examined. Compared to SZPs-HE, SZPs-APA showed greater surface area changes in the left superior frontal, right precentral and right cuneus cortices. Separately, within SZPs-APA, VO2max improvement was associated with changes in the left precentral and inferior temporal cortices and right insula, while reductions in apathy and positive symptoms were associated with changes in the right fusiform, rostral middle frontal, inferior temporal cortices and left supramarginal cortex. Greater FC changes within the frontoparietal network (FPN) were observed in e-APA versus e-HE, and within the default-mode network in SZPs-APA versus SZPs-HE, at the uncorrected level (neither survived multiple-comparison correction). FPN changes were associated with VO2max gains. No significant structural and functional differences occurred between SZPs-APA and HCs-APA. e-APA induced cortical plasticity in motor, visual, and associative regions in SZPs. Brain changes were associated with improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness and clinical symptoms, while uncorrected FC findings require cautious interpretation. e-APA may represent a promising adjunct to the treatment of schizophrenia.

item.title: Resting-state frontostriatal dysconnectivity and cognitive impairment in alcohol use disorder.
item.description:
Psychiatry research. Neuroimaging
Alcohol use disorder (AUD) involves persistent craving and cognitive deficits, reflecting an imbalance between reward/habit systems and cognitive control. This study used resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) to identify prefrontal-striatal circuits related to cognitive and clinical dimensions in AUD. Sixty-six male patients with AUD and 43 male healthy controls completed craving assessments, MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery testing, and resting-state fMRI. Seed-based rsFC analyses were conducted for the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), nucleus accumbens, and dorsal striatum (DS). Group differences and correlations with cognition and craving were examined. Compared with controls, patients with AUD showed poorer speed of processing, working memory, and reasoning/problem solving (all p < .05), but not verbal or visual learning. AUD was characterized by hypoconnectivity of DS and DLPFC with frontoparietal, temporal, and cerebellar regions. Within AUD, greater craving was associated with lower left DS-right supramarginal gyrus connectivity (r = -.267, p = .030). Poorer speed of processing was associated with greater right DLPFC-left orbital inferior frontal gyrus connectivity (r = -.289, p = .030). Poorer visual learning was associated with greater right DLPFC connectivity with the right middle temporal gyrus (r = -.268, p = .036) and right inferior temporal gyrus (r = -.259, p = .044). AUD involves widespread DS- and DLPFC-related hypoconnectivity and distinct circuit-level associations with craving and cognition. These preliminary findings provide initial support for a dimensional circuit-based framework of AUD heterogeneity and suggest that right DLPFC-related connectivity may be relevant to cognitive dysfunction. However, these associations were exploratory and require independent replication before any intervention implications can be considered.

item.title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.

item.title: Decoding individual differences in mental information from human brain responses predicted by deep neural networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Brain decoding using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has high potential for evaluating unobservable mental information that varies across individuals in everyday situations. Although estimating individual differences in mental information using brain decoding could be effective for social applications, especially in neuromarketing, the physical constraints and high costs of fMRI limit the practical application in real-world settings. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework to estimate individual differences in decodable mental information using brain responses predicted by deep neural networks (DNNs). In this framework, DNN-based models are trained to predict fMRI responses to natural movie scenes. Then, additional fMRI measurements are no longer required because mental information for new movie scenes can be decoded from the predicted responses instead of the measured ones. A large-scale analysis revealed that the proposed predicted-response decoding captures individual difference patterns consistent with those derived from conventional measured-response decoding across various cognitive domains. Of the 88 cognitive labels associated with movie scenes, individual difference patterns could be captured for more than 70% of the labels. This framework offers a promising approach for evaluating personal mental information with substantially reduced reliance on fMRI, thereby expanding the potential for social applications of brain decoding.

item.title: Insular subregional dysfunction in panic disorder: A multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background The spatial organization of insular abnormalities across connectional-architecture-defined subregions in panic disorder (PD) remains unclear. We examined structural and resting-state functional measures using the Brainnetome Atlas. Methods Forty-nine medication-naïve patients with PD and Fifty healthy controls underwent structural and resting-state MRI. Gray matter volume (GMV), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) were assessed across six insular subregions. Four prespecified functional connections were examined, together with exploratory Granger causality analysis between dIg and S1 and an AAL3 whole-insula comparison. Results dIg-S1 functional connectivity was reduced in PD (β = -0.148, 95% CI [-0.248, -0.048], pFDR = 0.017). ALFF showed a Group × Subregion interaction (F(5,578) = 4.162, p = 0.001). Only the ventral agranular insula (vIa) showed significantly higher ALFF after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (pFDR = 0.016), with a larger group effect than other subregions. The interaction persisted after temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) adjustment (F(5,577) = 2.582, p = 0.025), but the vIa-specific effect was nonsignificant in a separate vIa-only tSNR-adjusted model (p = 0.194). ReHo was directionally lower across all six subregions, but no contrast survived FDR correction. No robust subregional GMV differences or significant group differences in exploratory Granger causality were detected. Adjusted AAL3 whole-insula differences were nonsignificant. Conclusions PD showed measure-dependent insular functional alterations, including reduced dIg-S1 coupling and vIa-predominant ALFF differences, with the latter sensitive to signal quality and spatial smoothing.

item.title: Infant Negative Affect During Mother-Infant Interaction Is Associated with Neonatal Limbic-Prefrontal Connectivity in the First Month of Life.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
Background Early caregiving may shape neonatal limbic circuit organization, yet whether microanalytically coded interaction quality relates to neonatal limbic-prefrontal connectivity is unknown. We tested associations between infant and maternal affect during mother-infant interaction and neonatal limbic-prefrontal cortex (PFC) connectivity. Methods At approximately 30 days postnatal, 143 mother-infant dyads from the Healthy MiNDS cohort (São Paulo, Brazil) completed a video-recorded interaction coded with the Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB) system; infant negative affect was the percentage of interaction time in distress. Neonates underwent resting-state fMRI; limbic-PFC connectivity was quantified by principal component analysis of amygdala and hippocampus seed-to-ROI maps. Covariate-adjusted regressions tested associations. Results Infant negative affect was associated with right amygdala-PFC (β = -0.247, p = .003) and right hippocampus-PFC connectivity (β = -0.202, p = .021), both surviving FDR correction and robust across multiple analytic approaches. The amygdala association was limited to infant distress-related behaviors, whereas maternal positive expressiveness showed an independent, opposing association (β = 0.202, p = .019); no other CIB measure was significant. Exploratorily, connectivity was associated with sleep problems at 18-24 months in females (r = -.324, p = .030). Conclusions The emotional quality of early caregiving is associated with neonatal limbic circuit organization: infant distress is selectively associated with weaker amygdala-PFC connectivity, whereas maternal positive affect shows an independent opposing association. These findings identify the mother-infant relationship as a modifiable input to neonatal brain development.
